name: Umar Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential. Could you walk me through an ordinary shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the blast-hole drilling shift at a large phosphate mine and take the rig when the rock is uneven. We drill the holes before the blasting crew loads them, so a wrong angle can give the next team a bad day. My two-year technical diploma and years on the rig made me good at reading the ground, but I still check the cuttings with my own eyes. My wife Lidia takes tailoring orders from home, our children are grown, and we have four months of expenses saved. There is a small house loan left, and I hope to retire at 65. I use AI every day to compare drill vibration notes, then inspect the bit myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a quicker drill log is useful, provided the operator still checks the bit and the hole. A screen cannot taste the dust that tells me the rock has changed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my lead shifts to continue and Lidia's sewing orders to bring in a little extra. Four months saved covers a short stoppage, and this modest change should leave our house loan on schedule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep checking each drill bit before the shift and use my AI notes tool to sort recurring vibration faults. In the first year I'll teach apprentices how to compare a suggested bit change with the rig's service book.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about our wages. I am glad to spend less time copying numbers, so long as I still get to make the stop call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When did the AI note point to the wrong fault?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The AI tool once read a hard-rock vibration as a worn bearing. I pulled the bit and saw the crushed edge before we drilled the next hole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the house payment change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Lidia we can keep the house payment and visit our grown children as planned. A faster log is not a reason to spend the reserve.

say: I would welcome **quicker drill logs** while operators inspect the bit and hole.
I would tell the crew **rock dust** can reveal a change before a screen does.
think: I expect my **lead shifts** and Lidia’s tailoring orders to continue.
I think our **four-month cushion** covers a short stoppage without changing the house payment.
do: **Keep inspecting** drill bits before the shift and comparing AI faults with the service book.
**Teach apprentices** in the first year to verify suggested bit changes against the rig record.
feel: **Calm** about pay and pleased to spend less time copying drill figures.
S0.quote: A screen cannot taste the dust that tells me the rock has changed.
fieldNote: His **daily AI use** is checked against bit wear, dust and the rig service book.
A **four-month reserve** and continuing lead shifts make routine log automation manageable for the household.

steps.text: Keep inspecting drill bits before each shift
Teach apprentices to verify AI bit suggestions against rig service records

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say planning and parts orders will change before robots can drill a blast hole. I would like to see the new hole plan myself and show where the rig needs a wider turn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think fewer planners may make each operator carry more of the checking, and management could tighten our targets. My own lead pay looks safe, but a rushed hole can trouble the blasting crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll test the planning tool on last year's bore maps this month and mark holes that would have met an old seam. In the first year I'll ask the blast lead to check those marks with me before a live plan reaches the rig.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel interested in the tool and uneasy about a rushed handoff to blasting. A neat map is only the beginning of the ground check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you reject a suggested hole?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the plan puts a hole beside an old void, I'd stop and bring the blast lead out to the marker. The rig can wait while we find the true edge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach a new driller?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd teach the youngest driller how to mark the cuttings in a paper bag. A machine record is useful, but they need to know what the ground actually gave us.

say: I would expect **planning and ordering** to change before robots work the drilling rig.
I would ask to **check new hole plans** against the actual turning space and old seams.
think: I expect my **lead wage** to hold, though tighter targets could rush the drilling crew.
I worry a **bad hole** could endanger the blasting crew after my shift.
do: **Test the planning tool** this month against last year’s bore maps.
**Check marked holes** with the blast lead before a live plan reaches the rig.
feel: **Interested** in new planning tools and uneasy about a hurried blast handoff.
S1.quote: A neat map is only the beginning of the ground check.
fieldNote: He learns **planning software** early but validates it against old seams and actual rig turning space.
He expects **desk tasks** to shift before capable robots handle drilling; his own pay remains secure here.

steps.text: Test the planning tool against last year’s bore maps
Keep checking proposed holes with the blast lead before drilling

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the drillers full thinking AI by 2028 could write the plans, while capable drilling robots follow around 2031. I want the mine to offer a paid controls course before it cuts rig posts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 63 when robots arrive, two years before I planned to retire. Four months saved and my wife's uneven sewing orders would not carry two years of house payments and groceries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the mine for the price and schedule of its controls course this winter, then put a fixed part of each bonus payment into the house loan. In the first year after thinking AI arrives, I'll take the course only if the mine covers the fee and my wages, and apply for a posted controls job only if it pays close to drilling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about losing the final two years of rig pay, but I can work on a route now. I would rather earn by running equipment than make our grown children finance my last stretch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which household purchase would wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Lidia to pause the new sewing machine until we have written course and job terms. Her work matters, but I won't spend our four-month reserve on an uncertain post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the course real training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the instructor whether I get to stop a live rig when the hole drifts. If the course is only videos, I won't leave paid shifts for it.

say: I would separate **2028 planning AI** from capable drilling robots around 2031.
I would ask for a **paid controls course** before rig posts are cut.
think: I think at **63**, I could lose two years of rig wages before planned retirement.
I think our **four-month savings** and irregular sewing orders cannot cover that whole gap.
do: **Pay extra** on the house loan from each bonus payment starting now.
**Take controls training** after thinking AI arrives only with mine-paid fees and maintained wages.
**Delay the sewing machine** purchase until course and job terms are written.
feel: **Anxious** about losing final rig wages, with a conditional path through controls work.
S2.quote: Four months saved and my wife's uneven sewing orders would not carry two years of house payments and groceries.
fieldNote: His **2031 age** is 63, two years before his intended retirement at 65.
The **controls course** needs paid fees, wages and live rig practice; any job move needs a posted near-pay opening.

steps.text: Pay extra on the house loan from each bonus payment
Take controls training if mine covers fees and wages with live rig practice
Delay the sewing machine purchase until course and job terms are written
Apply for a posted controls role only if pay stays near drilling wages

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI by 2031 changes drill plans, while capable drilling robots arrive around 2034. Five years is enough to test controls work before deciding whether I need another mine post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 66 when robots arrive, one year after the age I hope to retire. That sounds easier, but I still need the pension to cover our house loan and usual bills before I hand back the rig keys.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll take the mine's short controls course if it has paid live-rig practice and a place for me. In the first year after thinking AI arrives, I'll keep leading the drill shift and ask the retirement office for a written pension figure at 65.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel fairly calm about the robot date and cautious about the pension. I can learn the controls without promising the family another career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the pension falls short?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the pension at 65 is short, I'd look for a posted drill shift at one of the nearby mines. I would not move house for a vague promise when Lidia's customers are here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you pass on to apprentices?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A real rig teaches more than a screen badge. I'd tell the apprentices that before the course starts. I want them to make a safe stop before I leave.

say: I would expect **2034 drill robots** after my hoped-for retirement at 65.
I would use the **five-year window** for paid practice on real controls.
think: I think at **66**, robots arrive after my planned finish, if the pension covers bills.
I will not return **rig keys** until house and food costs fit the written pension.
do: **Take the controls course** this year only with paid live-rig practice and an available place.
**Keep leading** drilling after thinking AI arrives and request a written pension figure at 65.
feel: **Fairly calm** about the robot date, with care about pension adequacy.
S3.quote: A real rig teaches more than a screen badge.
fieldNote: His **2034 age** is 66, after hoped-for retirement at 65.
He will **train only** with paid live-rig practice and a place, while a pension shortfall could lead to local job search.

steps.text: Take controls training if paid live-rig practice and a place are offered
Keep leading drill shifts after thinking AI arrives if work continues
Request written pension income for retirement at 65

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI by 2036 changes planning first, and capable drilling robots follow around 2039. Those dates are for younger drillers if the pension lets me finish at 65.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 68 when thinking AI arrives and 71 when robots come. We have four months saved, so I won't call retirement secure until the written pension covers our bills, but the robot date itself is not close to my working years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep the current house payment and drill shift while work is available. In the first year after thinking AI arrives, if retired as planned, I'll review the pension budget with Lidia and join the mine's apprenticeship group as a volunteer instructor if it offers a place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the late machines and still practical about money. I would like to hand the rig on to someone who has made mistakes under supervision rather than alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if pension income is too low?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the pension falls below our bills, I will ask about an actual posted drilling shift before dipping into the reserve. Nearby mines give some chance, not a guarantee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What lesson would you give apprentices?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the apprentices to look at the cuttings before trusting the plan. A wrong drilling angle can follow the blasting crew long after my shift ends.

say: I would see **2039 robots** as later than my hoped-for retirement.
I would support **paid apprenticeships** with supervised drilling practice.
think: I think at **68 and 71**, I expect retirement if the pension covers house and food bills.
I think our **four-month reserve** still needs protecting if the pension falls short.
do: **Keep drilling** and making the current house payment while shifts are available.
**Review pension bills** with Lidia after 2036 if retired as planned.
**Join the apprenticeship group** as a volunteer instructor after 2036 if it offers a place.
feel: **Calm** about robot timing and practical about the pension and apprentices’ training.
S4.quote: A wrong drilling angle can follow the blasting crew long after my shift ends.
fieldNote: His **2036 and 2039 ages** are 68 and 71, beyond planned retirement.
He may join the **apprenticeship group** as a volunteer instructor only if offered a place, while retirement still depends on pension income.

steps.text: Keep drilling shifts and making house payments while work lasts
Review written pension income against bills after 2036 if retired
Join the mine apprenticeship group as volunteer instructor if offered a place

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because drilling robots around 2031 could take two final earning years from me. A mine-funded course with live rig practice and a posted controls job at similar pay would help me keep the house plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who teaches a young driller when a bit wanders. An experienced operator beside a new driller can stop the first wrong hole before blasting begins. A training video cannot stop the rig.

headlineQuote: An experienced operator beside a new driller can stop the first wrong hole before blasting begins.
portrait: **Umar Alvarez**, 58, leads blast-hole drilling at a large phosphate mine and holds a two-year technical diploma.
He uses **AI daily** for vibration records but checks bits, cuttings and ground conditions himself.
He has **four months saved**, typical mine pay, a small house loan and a partner with variable tailoring income.
He hopes to **retire at 65**, making 2031 drilling robots at 63 a threat to two final earning years.
He seeks **mine-funded controls training** with live practice and would only take a posted role at near-current pay.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most because capable drilling robots could arrive two years before planned retirement.
whatWouldHelp: A **mine-funded controls course** and posted near-pay role would help him protect the house payment.
